Losar Guthuk (Tibetan Symbolic Dumpling Soup)

Served at: Losar (Tibetan New Year)

Serves 6-8Prep 60 minCook 45 min

Guthuk is a traditional Tibetan noodle soup, famously eaten on Gutor, the eve of Losar (Tibetan New Year). This special soup features hand-pulled dough pieces and small dumplings, some of which contain hidden symbolic items. The items are meant to playfully reveal one's character or fortune for the upcoming year, making it a fun and meaningful communal meal.

Ingredients

  • 3 cups (360g) all-purpose flour, plus more for dusting
  • 1 cup (240ml) warm water, plus more if needed
  • 1 teaspoon salt, divided
  • 8 cups (1.9L) beef or vegetable broth
  • 1 large daikon radish, peeled and cut into 1/2-inch (1.25 cm) cubes
  • 1-inch (2.5 cm) piece fresh ginger, peeled and thinly sliced
  • 3 cloves garlic, minced
  • 1 cup (70g) chopped fresh spinach or bok choy (optional)
  • 2 scallions, thinly sliced for garnish
  • A small piece of wool (bal)
  • A small dried chili pepper (se)
  • A pinch of extra salt (tsa)
  • A small piece of coal (sol)
  • A clean coin (ngul)
  • A small pebble (do)
  • A small piece of sugar (kar)
  • Other small, clean, non-toxic symbolic items as desired (e.g., a small piece of wood, cloth)

Method

  1. In a large bowl, combine the flour and 1/2 teaspoon of salt. Gradually add the warm water, mixing until a shaggy dough forms. Knead on a lightly floured surface for 5-7 minutes until smooth and elastic. Cover with a damp cloth and let rest for at least 30 minutes.
  2. While the dough rests, prepare the broth. In a large pot, combine the broth, daikon radish, ginger, garlic, and the remaining 1/2 teaspoon of salt. Bring to a boil, then reduce heat and simmer gently for 20 minutes, or until the radish is tender.
  3. Prepare your symbolic items. Ensure they are clean and clearly distinguishable. Set them aside.
  4. Divide the rested dough into two equal portions. On a lightly floured surface, roll out one portion into a thin sheet, about 1/8-inch (3mm) thick. Cut the dough into small, irregular, bite-sized pieces (about 1-inch/2.5 cm squares or triangles) for the 'noodles'.
  5. From the second portion of dough, pinch off small pieces and roll them into pea-sized balls. These will be your symbolic dumplings. For some of these small dough balls, carefully press one symbolic item into the center and seal the dough around it, forming a small, distinct dumpling. Make sure to keep track of which dumplings contain which symbols if you wish.
  6. Add the plain dough pieces (noodles) to the simmering broth. Cook for 5 minutes.
  7. Add the symbolic dumplings to the broth. If using, add the spinach or bok choy now. Continue to simmer for another 5-7 minutes, or until all dough pieces are cooked through and float to the surface.
  8. Ladle the Guthuk into individual bowls, ensuring each person receives a mix of noodles and symbolic dumplings. Garnish with sliced scallions and serve hot. As each person eats, they discover their symbolic item, leading to laughter and predictions for the New Year.

Tips

  • The meanings of common symbols: Wool (bal) for kindness, Chili (se) for being talkative, Salt (tsa) for laziness, Coal (sol) for having a 'dark heart', Coin (ngul) for prosperity, Pebble (do) for stubbornness, Sugar (kar) for sweetness.
  • For a vegetarian version, use vegetable broth and ensure all symbolic items are plant-based or inert.
  • The dough should be firm but pliable. If it's too sticky, add a little more flour; if too dry, add a tiny bit more water.
